The Call of the Wild
Robert W. Service (1907) · from “The Call of the Wild,” stanza 4, lines 1–4
· · ·
Have you suffered, starved and triumphed, groveled down, yet grasped at glory, Grown bigger in the bigness of the whole? "Done things" just for the doing, letting babblers tell the story, Seeing through the nice veneer the naked soul?
· · ·
groveled: crawled low, or begged · grasped at: reached hard for · babblers: people who talk on and on · veneer: a thin, shiny surface that hides what is under it · naked soul: a person as they truly are

✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Model
My coach said, “Run the last lap hard.”

A comma comes before the quotation. The speaker’s exact words sit inside quotation marks and begin with a capital letter, and the period goes inside the closing mark.

🔧 Fix this one
john thornton said never was there such a dog
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

John Thornton said, “Never was there such a dog.” John Thornton is a name, so each part takes a capital letter. A comma comes before the quotation, quotation marks surround the spoken words, the first spoken word takes a capital, and the period goes inside the closing mark.

🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Sentence edges, quotations, and cut words
Professor Lovelore At the board
0:45
An AI-generated character and voice.
1. Sentence edges
A fragment is half a sentence.
A run-on jams two sentences together.
A comma splice joins them with only a comma.
Fix it with a period, a semicolon, or a comma and a word like and, but, so.
2. Quotations
Copy London word for word and mark for mark.
The citation comes after the closing quotation mark. The period comes after the citation.
Buck became “a thing of the wild” (London, Ch. 7).
3. Cut words
Cut words from the middle of a quotation? Three dots show where.
Never change a quoted word.

Tap each mark where one complete sentence ends and the next begins. London, Chapter VII

Tap the mark where one complete sentence ends and the next begins. London, Chapter VII
The wolf was suspicious and afraid; for Buck made three of him in weight, while his head barely reached Buck’s shoulder.
Tap the mark where one complete sentence ends and the next begins. London, Chapter VII
Fish, in open pools, were not too quick for him; nor were beaver, mending their dams, too wary.
Tap the mark where one complete sentence ends and the next begins. London, Chapter VII
He killed to eat, not from wantonness; but he preferred to eat what he killed himself.
London often puts a semicolon before for or but. Writers did that in 1903. In your essay, use a semicolon alone, or a comma before and, but or so.
Tap the comma that belongs to the quotation. London, Chapter VII

🔤 Match All Ten Words
Five from the first half of the chapter, five from the ending.
obliterated
Wiped out so completely that no trace is left
tangible
Real enough to be touched
impelled
Driven or pushed to act, by a force inside or outside
pertinacity
Stubborn refusal to give up
infinitesimal
So small it can hardly be measured
✨ All five matched.
void
An empty space left where something used to be
cessation
A stopping or ending
compellingly
In a way that is very hard to resist
agility
The ability to move quickly and easily
discomfited
Beaten back and thrown into confusion
✨ All five matched.

Edit your essay: three passes
  1. Read it aloud: one sentence at a time. Where your voice runs out of breath, look for a run-on or a comma splice. Where it stops too soon, look for a fragment.
  2. Check every quotation: against the book, word for word and mark for mark, and check every citation.
  3. Add one transition: a sentence that shows how two paragraphs connect.
Show each fix before and after
🪶 Sentence frames you can borrow

Fix an edge: ___, because ___. · ___; ___. · ___, and ___.

Quote and cite: London writes, “___” (Ch. 7). · Buck was “___” when ___ (London, Ch. 7).

Connect two paragraphs: Still, ___. · In the end, ___. · That is why ___.
